1.pericope_label: If there be a controversy between men, and they come unto judgment, that the judges may judge them; then they shall justify the righteous, and condemn the wicked. And it shall be, if the wicked man be worthy to be beaten, that the judge shall cause him to lie down, and to be beaten before his face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes he may give him, and not exceed: lest, if he should exceed, and beat him above these with many stripes, then thy brother should seem vile unto thee.

schools.summary: Read the whole provision as a restraint on zeal rather than a schedule of penalties, since no equal measure is prescribed and judges otherwise not unjust are often as severe on small offences as on crimes; the requirement that the judge be present is there so that his authority may prevent excess. Argue the case outward: since God spares the guilty so far as to repress even just severity, much more will he have regard to innocent blood, and much less will he tolerate private violence between brothers. Then give the rabbinic mechanics of the reduction to thirty-nine — the number read as the one next to forty, and the scourge made with three lashes so that thirteen strokes made thirty-nine while a fourteenth would have overshot by two — and note that the apostle suffered the full extremity of it as then understood.

Treat the opening clause as a key to passages elsewhere, since the Hebrew verb for justify is used exactly as the corresponding Greek verb is sometimes used by Paul, not to make just but to acquit, to declare innocent, to remit punishment; the magistrates are to acquit the righteous, and the Greek version uses the very word Paul uses of a sinner's justification. Report the procedure of beating in the judge's presence as it survives in China, where the magistrate sees the letter of the law fulfilled and the officers transgress it neither by indulgence nor by severity. Call the reduction to thirty-nine prudent caution rather than superstition, lest through mistake or forgetfulness they pass a bound they were commanded to keep; and use the verse for a long protest against sentences of three hundred or a thousand lashes.

Supply the physical detail the text leaves out: the strokes were administered with a stick upon the back, and the posture can be identified from Egyptian monuments, where the culprit lies flat upon the ground, is held fast by hands and feet, and receives the strokes in the presence of the judge. Explain the idiom, that a son of stripes means a man liable to them, as a son of death means one liable to die, and that the phrase about number means as many stripes as the crime deserved. Make the reason for the limit both medical and social, since more strokes would endanger health and life and would also disgrace the man, and add that one who deserved worse was to be executed rather than beaten further.

Set out the procedure the first verse presupposes: accuser and accused brought face to face before the judges, acquittal where the proof falls short, and, where the charge is made out, the conviction of the accused counting as a justification of the accuser as righteous in the prosecution — with the reciprocal principle from Proverbs that justifying the wicked is as much an abomination as condemning the righteous. Note that a great many precepts carry no stated penalty, and that by constant Jewish practice the breach of these was punished with scourging, from which no person's rank exempted him; and that the beating was to be done solemnly, not tumultuously through the streets but in open court before the judge's face.

debates.question: What does justify the righteous mean here?

sides.position: To acquit, declare innocent, remit punishment — the same use Paul makes of the corresponding Greek verb of a sinner's justification
To acquit from guilt and false accusation and free from punishment
A verdict that also justifies the accuser as righteous in the prosecution when the charge is made out

debates.question: Why is the number limited to forty?

sides.position: So that the body torn by the whip should not be maimed or disfigured, and so that judges, often as severe on small offences as on crimes, should be restrained
Because more strokes would endanger health and life and also disgrace the man; one who deserved worse was to be executed instead
Either because the usage itself made him contemptible, or because of the deformity excessive beating might produce

debates.question: Why did the Jews stop at thirty-nine?

sides.position: The rabbinic rule reads the number as the one next to forty, and the three-lashed scourge made thirteen strokes come to thirty-nine exactly
Prudent caution, not superstition, lest through mistake or forgetfulness they pass a bound they were commanded to keep

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a lexical key for Paul, arguing that the Hebrew verb and the Greek verb of justification alike mean to acquit rather than to make just; and alone reports the same courtroom procedure surviving in China.
Alone identifies the posture of the beating from Egyptian monuments, where the culprit lies flat on the ground held fast by hands and feet.

themes: justify the righteous and condemn the wicked
forty stripes he may give him
lest thy brother seem vile unto thee

4.pericope_label: Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn.

schools.summary: Collect what else the prohibition covers, since a muzzle is only one way of keeping a working animal from the grain: putting a thorn in the creature's mouth, causing a lion to lie down beside it, causing its calf to lie down outside the floor, spreading a skin over the top of the corn, or besmearing the ox's nostrils with cow dung, which the animal found so disagreeable that it would not feed. Then justify the apostolic use of the verse: Paul is its faithful expositor, declaring that God had no other design than that the labourer should not be defrauded of his hire, and himself meeting the objection that oxen and men differ by saying that God does not care for oxen but spoke for the sake of those who labour. Do not let the literal sense drop out even so, since men are instructed in equity to the point of being bound to exercise it toward brute animals.

Fill in the practice from travellers: mules and horses were often used instead of oxen, three or four tied by the neck and whipped round the floor; the work was done in the open air on a level plot daubed over with cow dung to keep down the dust, so that earth and gravel were taken up with the grain and the straw shattered — a circumstance alluded to where a king is said to have made Israel like the dust by threshing. Report from Bengal that some muzzle the ox and some do not, according to the farmer's disposition. Take the precept as symbolical, teaching kindness to servants and labourers and especially to those who minister in holy things, and note that one commentator holds it wholly symbolical; or simply say that God taught humanity here to the beasts that serve us, and much more to the men who labour for us.

Describe the threshing the precept assumes — oxen yoked together and driven to and fro over corn strewn on the floor so that the grains are kicked out by their hoofs — and report that both the method and the custom of leaving the animals unmuzzled survive in the East, adding drily that the Mosaic injunctions are not so strictly observed there by the Christians as by the Mohammedans. Then call the sentence proverbial in its nature rather than a rule about oxen only, to be understood in the general sense the apostle gives it, that a labourer is not to be deprived of his wages.

Take it as a charge to husbandmen, teaching us to make much of the animals that serve us; but learn from it not only to be just but to be kind to all who are employed for the good of our better part, our souls.

debates.question: Is the precept about oxen or about men?

sides.position: Proverbial in nature, to be understood in the general sense the apostle gives it, that a labourer is not to be deprived of his wages
Symbolical, teaching kindness to servants and labourers and especially to those who minister in holy things — one commentator holding it wholly symbolical
About both: God had no other design than that the labourer not be defrauded, yet men are bound to exercise equity even toward brute animals
A charge to husbandmen first, teaching us to make much of the animals that serve us, and then to be kind to those employed for the good of our souls

outliers.note: Alone collects the other devices the prohibition covers, from Maimonides the thorn in the mouth, the lion couched beside the ox, the calf laid down outside and the skin spread over the corn, and from Aelian the besmearing of the nostrils with cow dung.

Alone reports the threshing floor as it was actually worked, daubed with cow dung against the dust, and finds in the shattered straw the point of the saying that a king made Israel like the dust by threshing.

themes: thou shalt not muzzle the ox

5.pericope_label: If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger: her husband’s brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband’s brother unto her. And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name be not put out of Israel. And if the man like not to take his brother’s wife, then let his brother’s wife go up to the gate unto the elders, and say, My husband’s brother refuseth to raise up unto his brother a name in Israel, he will not perform the duty of my husband’s brother. Then the elders of his city shall call him, and speak unto him: and if he stand to it, and say, I like not to take her; Then shall his brother’s wife come unto him in the presence of the elders, and loose his shoe from off his foot, and spit in his face, and shall answer and say, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother’s house. And his name shall be called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

schools.summary: Read the word for brother against its plain sense, since it means not actual brothers but cousins and other kinsmen whose marriage with the widow would not have been incestuous — otherwise God would contradict himself, having forbidden a man to uncover his brother's nakedness — and take Boaz for proof, who married Ruth not as the brother of her deceased husband but as his near kinsman. Make the law a property provision above all, since its object is that no one be obliged to leave what he has to strangers, and God so far provides even for the dying that what they could not resign without regret is preserved to their offspring; on this reading a kinsman who fails to obviate the childlessness commits a kind of theft, childlessness being a curse and a borrowed offspring the only consolation in it. Then supply the procedure around the loosing of the shoe, the time and place appointed the evening before by three rabbins and two witnesses, and the woman ordered to come fasting; and note that the name of infamy afterwards attached not to the man only but to his house.

Make the residence requirement practical, that if the next brother had moved to remote parts or been carried into captivity the widow was free to marry the next kinsman living where she was; and add a purpose peculiar to the nation, that the distinction of tribes and families be kept up so that the Messiah might be discovered by the family from which he was appointed to proceed, and the distinction of inheritances with it. On the ceremony, explain the shoe as a sign of right and power, so that parting with it was a token of the alienation of that right, and add the second edge, that going barefoot was the condition of the meanest servants, so that the loosing marked the man unworthy to be among freemen. Correct the English of the spitting, reporting that the Jews, the legitimate judges in the case, hold it was not into the face but before the face on the ground, which is how detestation is still expressed in the East.

Give the mechanism exactly: the first-born was to stand upon the name of the deceased, that is, be placed in the family of the dead man and recognised as the heir of his property, so that his name should not be blotted out of Israel; and note that the verb used is denominative, formed from the noun for a husband's brother, so that it means literally to act the brother-in-law.

Note that the usage is ancient, appearing already in the story of Judah's family, and that the widow was not to marry into another family unless all her husband's relations refused her, so that the estate she was endowed with should not be alienated. Give both sides of the kindness intended, toward her, who having forgotten her own people should have all possible kindness from the family into which she married, and toward the deceased, that though dead he might not be forgotten nor lost out of the genealogies of his tribe. Then supply the human reason underneath: under that dispensation men had no such clear and certain prospect of living beyond death as the gospel has since given, and were therefore the more desirous to live in their posterity, an innocent desire which this law in some measure gratified.

sides.position: No — cousins and other kinsmen whose marriage would not be incestuous, since Boaz married Ruth as a near kinsman and not as a brother
Yes, and brothers on the father's side only, since there is no brotherhood but on the father's side
The brother-in-law, the verb being formed from the noun for a husband's brother
Living in the same house, brothers brought up together in their father's house
Being united in one inheritance, so that the place of residence does not matter
The same town or at least the same country; if the next brother had moved far off or been carried into captivity, the widow was free
That no one be obliged to leave his property to strangers; the kinsman who fails to obviate the childlessness commits a kind of theft
That the first-born stand upon the name of the deceased, placed in his family and recognised as heir, so his name not be blotted out
That the distinction of tribes and families be kept up, so the Messiah might be discovered by the family from which he was to come
That men who had no clear prospect of living beyond death might live in their posterity, an innocent desire this law gratified

outliers.note: Alone denies that the word brother is to be taken literally, arguing from the incest laws that God would otherwise contradict himself, and citing Boaz as a kinsman rather than a brother.

Alone supplies the reason underneath the custom, that men under that dispensation had no such clear prospect of living beyond death as the gospel has since given, and were therefore the more desirous to live in their posterity.

themes: raise up seed unto his brother
loose his shoe from off his foot

11.pericope_label: When men strive together one with another, and the wife of the one draweth near for to deliver her husband out of the hand of him that smiteth him, and putteth forth her hand, and taketh him by the secrets: Then thou shalt cut off her hand, thine eye shall not pity her. Thou shalt not have in thy bag divers weights, a great and a small. Thou shalt not have in thine house divers measures, a great and a small. But thou shalt have a perfect and just weight, a perfect and just measure shalt thou have: that thy days may be lengthened in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee. For all that do such things, and all that do unrighteously, are an abomination unto the Lord thy God.

schools.summary: Concede that the law is apparently harsh, and then argue that its severity is the point, showing how pleasing modesty is to God and how thoroughly he abominates indecency; call the act inexcusable effrontery, a wilful assault on the part of the body from whose sight and touch chaste women naturally recoil. Draw the inference by proportion: if the thing was punished so heavily in the heat of a quarrel, where agitation of mind is at least some excuse, then the same done deliberately out of lust would be pardoned still less, and judges were bound to reason the same way, from the less to the greater, whenever they punished obscenity. Assign the execution carefully to the civil magistrate rather than to the injured man or a bystander; and leave open whether the sentence was literal, reporting that the Jewish writers read it of a price set upon the hand and compare it with the law of retaliation, so that the hand is forfeit only if she does not redeem it.

Catch the force of the prohibition, that they were forbidden not merely to use false weights but to have them, not in the bag and not in the house, since possessing them is a standing temptation; and observe that the two together cheat at both ends, as with the prophet's ephah made small for selling corn and shekel made great for weighing the money received. Add the reason the passage gives, that what is the rule of justice must itself be just or it becomes a constant cheat, and set the promise of length of days against the sanction that not only unrighteousness but all who do unrighteously are an abomination.

Explain the weights, which are literally a stone and a stone, since weights were anciently made of stone and a dishonest trader kept two sets, a heavy one to buy his neighbour's wares by and a light one to sell his own; add that the practice was once common in Britain, where smooth round stones were chosen by country people for selling goods by the pound, and that the term a stone weight survives although lead or iron is now the counterpoise. Note that the measure named next is likewise doubled in the Hebrew, an ephah and an ephah, one large to buy with and one small to sell by, so that there were knaves in all ages and among all nations.

debates.question: Was the hand actually cut off?

sides.position: The Jewish writers read it of a valuable consideration, a price set upon the hand, comparing the law of retaliation; the hand is forfeit only if she does not redeem it
The severity is real and is the point, showing how thoroughly God abominates indecency; the added warning against pity exists so that judges should not be remiss in inflicting it

debates.question: Why forbid merely having false weights?

sides.position: Because possessing them is a standing temptation — not in the bag and not in the house
Because two sets were the trader's whole method, a heavy stone to buy by and a light one to sell by

outliers.note: Alone reasons from the case by proportion, that if the act was punished so heavily in the heat of a quarrel, where agitation is some excuse, the same done deliberately out of lust would be pardoned still less.
Alone traces the stone weights into recent British practice, where smooth round stones were used by country people and the term a stone weight survives although the counterpoise is now lead or iron.

themes: thine eye shall not pity her
divers weights, a great and a small

17.pericope_label: Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt; How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God. Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.

schools.summary: Count the aggravations rather than the offence: the attack was unjust in the first place, since Israel was inflicting neither injury nor loss and was merely passing peaceably toward another land, and it violated humanity still more grossly because the Amalekites did not spare their own kindred, being descendants of Esau and so sprung with Israel from the one ancestor. Concentrate on the clause that they feared not God, refusing to take it in its ordinary sense and reading it as deliberate rebellion, since the promise given to Abraham and Isaac could not have been unknown to them. Then meet the objection that the command sits ill with religion, since it appears to order retaliation: the people are not stimulated to vindictive feeling but commanded to punish the sins of Amalek with the same severity as those of other nations, and the intention of the Legislator must be judged by his nature, no angry or hateful passion being capable of God's approval. Finally, fix the timing, since rest from all enemies round about means freedom from the neighbouring nations too, so that the order took effect only in the reign of the first king.

Aggravate the offence from the condition of the victims, that this was done to a people long exercised with sore afflictions, to whom pity was owed by the laws of nature and humanity, and for whose rescue God had appeared so gloriously that the Amalekites could not have been ignorant of it, so that the act was barbarousness to Israel and a setting of the great Jehovah at defiance. Then carry the reckoning to its end, supposing the final accomplishment of the sentence to be the death of Haman and his ten sons, from which time the name of Amalek was blotted out from under heaven; and add that through every period of their history it might truly be said of them that they feared not God.

Set the passage in its place at the close of the whole discourse on the law, as the warning that while love was to be the guiding principle of Israel's dealings with a neighbour and even with strangers and foes, that love was not to degenerate into weakness or indifference toward open ungodliness; and locate the attack precisely at the rear of the column, among all the enfeebled who lagged behind when the people were faint and weary on the march out of Egypt.

Turn the case to warning and to allegory at once: let every persecutor and injurer of God's people take warning from it, since the longer it is before judgment comes the more dreadful it will be at last; and let Amalek remind us of the foes of our own souls, that we may be enabled to slay all our lusts and all the corruptions within and without which oppose our way to the Saviour.

debates.question: Does the command to blot out Amalek sanction revenge?

sides.position: No: the people are not stimulated to vindictive feeling but commanded to punish Amalek's sins with the same severity as those of other nations, and the Legislator's intention must be judged by his nature
It is a warning that love toward neighbour, stranger and foe was not to degenerate into weakness or indifference toward open ungodliness
It is a warning to every persecutor of God's people, and Amalek may stand for the foes of our own souls
Not after the conquest nor in the time of the judges, when Israel was harassed continually, but only in the reign of the first king
Finally in the death of Haman and his ten sons, from which time the name was blotted out from under heaven

outliers.note: Alone presses the kinship, that the Amalekites descended from Esau and so cast away the feelings of nature in attacking men sprung from the same ancestor; and alone reads the clause about not fearing God as deliberate rebellion rather than ordinary irreligion.
Alone dates the execution of the command, observing that rest from all enemies round about excludes the period of the judges and points to the reign of the first king.

themes: remember what Amalek did unto thee
he smote the hindmost of thee
blot out the remembrance of Amalek
